steps.action: Frame the long-standing debate over the origin and connectivity of the calcium-chloride groundwater brines in Wright Valley.
steps.quote: a long-standing debate as to the origin and connectivity of groundwater brines in the valley

steps.action: Report the DVDP-era hypothesis of a groundwater system flowing west from Lake Vanda.
steps.quote: hypothesized the presence of a groundwater system flowing from Lake Vanda to the west.

steps.action: Report that the westward-flow hypothesis was rejected on borehole fluid potentials and the frozen DVDP14 core.
steps.quote: They later invalidated this hypothesis based on fluid potentials measured in [...] .

steps.action: Report DVDP13 borehole observations at Don Juan Pond: water rising above the pond level, brine salinity, and artesian flow.
steps.quote: the pond was receiving groundwater discharge

steps.action: Lay out the rival sources: a confined Ferrar Dolerite aquifer fed from the ice sheet, versus surface brine generation by deliquescence and surface discharge.
steps.quote: the fractured and highly mineralized Ferrar Dolerite might be a confined aquifer

steps.action: Use expectations from others' work: mixing and brine-evolution models require a deep groundwater source, and elevations imply recharge from Don Juan Pond to Lake Vanda.
steps.quote: most mixing models predict that the salts in Lake Vanda and Don Juan Pond could not have originated solely from surface inputs

steps.action: State the aim: map the distribution of subsurface water and hydrological connectivity with non-destructive geophysics.
steps.quote: Our research goals were to map water distribution and hydrological connectivity

steps.action: Acquire helicopter-borne AEM data over Wright Valley in 2011 and 2018.
steps.quote: Here, we present data from AEM surveys flown in Wright Valley in 2011 and 2018

steps.action: Use the helicopter TEM system and survey methodology developed and characterized in the group's earlier papers, including a ground-based versus airborne comparison.
steps.quote: A comprehensive methodology on our 2018 AEM survey can be found in

steps.action: Invert the TEM signals to resistivity sections with 1D forward modeling (with an induced-polarization forward response at Don Juan Pond), and state footprint and depth of investigation.
steps.quote: Inversion is used to estimate the underlying electrical resistivity structures, consistent with observed TEM signals.

steps.action: Select three low-elevation E–W flight lines for analysis and set aside N–S lines because they show 3D effects that make the 1D inversion produce spurious features.
steps.quote: These flight lines were picked to align with the lowest-elevation tracks of Wright Valley, where one might assume brine would pool

steps.action: Check the line selection against additional higher-elevation E–W lines, which return higher resistivities.
steps.quote: Additional E–W flight lines along higher-elevation tracks returned higher resistivity readings

steps.action: Check the inverted Lake Vanda resistivity profile against the measured lake-water conductivity profile and the saline sediment water found in DVDP4A.
steps.quote: This is consistent with electrical conductivity (EC) of lake water in Vanda

steps.action: Explain the unexpectedly high 1 Ωm surface resistivity at Don Juan Pond by averaging over 4 m, sediment porosity, and CaCl2 conductivity behaviour, rather than revising the brine interpretation.
steps.quote: This might appear high for the second saltiest body of water on Earth, but the pond itself is only 20–30 cm deep

steps.action: Compare a second low-resistivity zone at 23–36 m under Don Juan Pond with the hypothesized Ferrar Dolerite aquifer depth.
steps.quote: This depth overlaps with the hypothesized aquifer in the Ferrar Dolerite

steps.action: Add independent salt-chemistry evidence from other work linking Ferrar Dolerite to Don Juan Pond brine.
steps.quote: This is yet another line of evidence that supports a connection between Ferrar Dolerite and Don Juan Pond brine.

steps.action: Propose that a vertical low-resistivity feature east of Don Juan Pond is a dolerite dyke reaching the VXE-6 pond basin.
steps.quote: This vertical feature (possibly a dolerite dyke) would intersect a surface basin which contains the VXE-6 pond.

steps.action: Keep regional connectivity within the Don Juan Pond basin, with brine on both sides of the pond lying above pond level, as the explanation for the artesian discharge.
steps.quote: In the Don Juan Pond basin, AEM data provide evidence for regional connectivity.

steps.action: Compare the expected valley-wide connection with the profiles: no conductors east of Lake Vanda, no shallow link to the Forks, shallow brines in the North Fork.
steps.quote: From our AEM survey, any valley-wide groundwater connectivity is obscure.

steps.action: Reconcile the frozen DVDP14 core with the detected North Fork brines by borehole depth or spatial heterogeneity.
steps.quote: DVDP14 did not penetrate the permafrost, and it may be that it did not extend deep enough

steps.action: Confirm the no-signal zone between Don Juan Pond and Lake Vanda with both the airborne and the ground-based TEM systems.
steps.quote: Neither survey was able to record a signal that exceeded the noise floor of the system

steps.action: Refine the connection hypothesis: any brine in the no-signal zone lies deeper than 500 m, and a dolerite conduit would not follow surface topography; no conclusion is drawn on an ice-sheet source.
steps.quote: If there is a dolerite conduit between the two surface waterbodies, it does not follow the surface topography.

steps.action: Compare the possible >500 m connection depth with AEM-inferred brines and frozen–unfrozen transitions in Taylor Valley boreholes.
steps.quote: This depth is in the range at which liquid brines were inferred in Taylor Valley from AEM

steps.action: Keep the presence of unfrozen brine-saturated subsurface regions, while leaving valley-wide connectivity unresolved.
steps.quote: did confirm the presence of unfrozen brine-saturated regions in the subsurface

end.claim: AEM resistivity sections show unfrozen brine-saturated regions beneath Lake Vanda, Don Juan Pond and the North Fork within the depth of investigation; valley-wide connectivity remains unresolved.

decisive_move.sentence: Inverting the helicopter TEM data into resistivity cross-sections is what turns the survey into a claim about subsurface brine.

gates.evidence: The surveys were flown 'in exploration of liquid water' (§0 ¶1). Lines were chosen where brine was assumed to pool (§2 ¶3), so the assumption, not a stated hypothesis test, directed line selection. Brine presence could have failed: no conductors were found east of Lake Vanda (§3 ¶5). The connectivity test was inconclusive. Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

limits: No review file or open discussion was supplied, although the acknowledgements say two reviewers' critiques 'significantly improved this paper' (p. 4981). Review-driven changes therefore cannot be coded, and no review sequence is given. Only three of the flown lines are shown. The N–S and higher-elevation lines are described but not displayed. Inversion regularisation, model uncertainty and data misfit are not reported here; they are deferred to Grombacher et al. 2021. The ground-based TEM data are referenced (Madsen et al. 2022) but not shown. Sub-claims and their statuses: (1) regional connectivity within the Don Juan Pond basin and the dolerite-dyke link to VXE-6 are best_explanation (§3 ¶3-4); (2) brine hosted in Ferrar Dolerite is best_explanation, called speculation (§0 ¶1, §4 ¶1); (3) valley-wide connectivity between Lake Vanda and Don Juan Pond has no conclusion (§4 ¶2); (4) the brine source and any ice-sheet connection have no conclusion (§3 ¶5). Composition is none_fits because the walk applies an inherited capability to a pre-existing question and maps what it finds. Rivals are cited but not set against a shared crucial test. It is neither capability-first (the question and rivals precede the survey) nor a trace series of independent repetitions (inference). Whether the 2011 data contribute to the three 2018 lines shown is not stated.

disagreements.target: The DVDP-era reading that the frozen DVDP14 core negated westward groundwater flow into the North Fork
disagreements.support: The AEM profiles show a layer of shallow brines in the North Fork; the authors argue DVDP14 was too shallow or missed a heterogeneous unfrozen layer.
disagreements.quote: DVDP14 did not penetrate the permafrost, and it may be that it did not extend deep enough

disagreements.target: The expectation of a regional system recharging from higher Don Juan Pond to lower Lake Vanda, and the 'follow the dolerite' idea with westward-dipping sills
disagreements.support: No shallow conductive link is seen, the area between the waterbodies returns no signal to the instruments' depth, and brine-saturated dolerite is absent at [...] eastern end of the South Fork transect.
disagreements.quote: If there is a dolerite conduit between the two surface waterbodies, it does not follow the surface topography.

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Additional higher-elevation E–W lines; N–S lines across Lake Vanda
alternatives_considered.reason: Low-elevation tracks are where brine might pool; higher lines returned higher resistivity; N–S lines show 3D effects that create spurious 'pant legs' under a 1D inversion

alternatives_considered.chosen: Standard 1D TEM forward modeling, with a more complex induced-polarization forward response at Don Juan Pond
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Standard 1D forward modeling at Don Juan Pond
alternatives_considered.reason: Strong induced polarization effects at Don Juan Pond

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Ground-based TEM with larger transmitter coils and longer stacking times
alternatives_considered.reason: none given for the choice; ground-based TEM could penetrate more deeply with potentially higher accuracy
